meta.tagline: One of the world's most expensive cities — most of the best things are free

pills: Ask for the Transport Card at check-in
Eat fondue in the right place

overview.intro: Geneva is a small city — but inside it sits the European headquarters of the United Nations, more than 40 international organisations, and the world's densest concentration of diplomatic missions. You notice it when you arrive: everything is too orderly, too clean, too quiet. After 10pm the streets empty. Then you sit on the shore of Lac Léman, the Alps across the water, the Jet d'Eau above, a coffee beside you — and you understand why the city was built here. At Jonction, two rivers meet in different colours. In Carouge, an Italian neighbourhood spirit starts to breathe. Geneva is small but layered.

local_word.definition: Half and half. In Geneva, when fondue is mentioned, this is what's meant: half Gruyère, half Vacherin Fribourgeois cheese. This is the standard blend. At a restaurant, don't just say 'fondue' — ask for 'moitié-moitié' and you'll notice the difference. A winter dish; from November to March.

rules.title: If you're staying in a hotel, all transport is free — ask at check-in
rules.description: If you're staying in a hotel, hostel or campsite in Geneva, you're entitled to a Geneva Transport Card. For the duration of your stay, tram, bus, train and the yellow ferry (Mouettes Genevoises) are all free. It covers the airport transfer too. Sometimes it doesn't arrive automatically — ask at check-in.

rules.title: An expensive city — but the free things are genuinely good
rules.description: Restaurant prices are among the highest in Europe; plan accordingly. But don't forget: the Jet d'Eau, the Reformation Wall, walking the Vieille Ville streets, walking to Jonction and the lakeside are all free. Many museums are free on Sundays. Lunch menus are often half the price of dinner at the same restaurant — same quality.

rules.title: Fondue and raclette are winter dishes — don't order them in summer
rules.description: November to March is the right season for fondue and raclette. In summer they're served at tourist restaurants, but these dishes belong to the cold. The right question in summer is: 'Do you have Filets de perches du Léman?' Fresh lake perch from Lac Léman — if the menu doesn't say 'du Léman', the fish may be frozen and imported from Eastern Europe.

tip.label: Geneveroule — free bike rental
tip.text: The Geneveroule office is directly across from Gare Cornavin. Leave your ID and a 20 CHF deposit, take a bike for the day. The deposit is returned at the end of the day; the bike is free. Geneva is the right size for cycling. The lakeside, Carouge and Plainpalais are all flat and bike-friendly. Season runs May to October.

overview.title: Welcome to Geneva

transport.intro: Geneva is small and well connected. Tram, bus, train and yellow ferry all run on the same ticket — and if you're staying in a hotel, it's all free.

items.title: Airport → City
items.description: From the train station in the basement of the airport to Gare Cornavin: 7 minutes, every 10-15 minutes. After collecting your baggage, show your boarding pass at the ticket machines to get a free 80-minute ticket. If you have the Geneva Transport Card, you don't need this — it's already free.

items.title: TPG — tram and bus
items.description: 6 tram lines (numbered 12-17) and a comprehensive bus network cover every corner of the city. A single ticket is valid for 60 minutes; free transfers between tram, bus, train and Mouettes. Tickets are bought at machines at stops — city buses have no machines on board, so buy before you get on.

items.title: Mouettes Genevoises — yellow ferry
items.description: Small yellow boats linking the two shores of the lake, on the same TPG ticket. Line M1 runs from Pâquis to Eaux-Vives, line M2 from near the Mont-Blanc Bridge to Genève-Plage. A short crossing, but over Lac Léman — the easiest way to see the city from a different angle.

items.title: Bike — Geneveroule
items.description: Directly across from Gare Cornavin. Leave your ID and a 20 CHF deposit for a free day bike. Flat, safe routes along the lakeside to Carouge and Plainpalais. Season May to October.

items.title: Walking — ideal for the city centre
items.description: Vieille Ville, Pâquis and the lakeside are all connected on foot. Gare Cornavin to the Jet d'Eau: 20 minutes. Carouge: 15 minutes by tram or 35 minutes on foot. Jonction: 25 minutes' walk from the centre.

callout.label: Geneva Transport Card — ask at check-in
callout.text: If you're staying in a hotel, hostel or campsite in Geneva, you're entitled to this card. It covers all TPG vehicles, trains and the Mouettes within Zone 10 for the duration of your stay. It sometimes isn't sent automatically — if you don't ask at check-in, you might miss it. Covers the airport transfer too. Public transport in Geneva isn't cheap; this card is a real saving.

transport.title: Getting Around

stay.intro: Geneva is small but its neighbourhoods are very different. Where you stay directly shapes how you experience the city.

local_word.definition: Planned by Sardinian architects in the 18th century, Carouge is technically part of Geneva but independent in spirit. The Italian influence is strong: wide courtyards, low-rise buildings, pavement cafés. Completely different from the city's cool, protocol-driven atmosphere. With its weekend market, local restaurants and evening atmosphere, it's Geneva's most alive corner.

items.name: Rive / Eaux-Vives
items.description: On the left bank of the lake, walking distance from the Jet d'Eau. The Jardin Anglais, shopping streets and the Halles de Rive food market are here. Easy tram connections everywhere. The right choice if it's your first time and you want easy access to everything.

items.name: Pâquis
items.description: Right next to Gare Cornavin, on the right bank of the lake. Geneva's most multicultural neighbourhood; Asian, African and Arab communities live here. Bains des Pâquis is the summer gathering point on the lakeside. Restaurants and bars stay open late — the least quiet part of the city.

items.name: Vieille Ville / Old Town
items.description: On top of the hill, with the Cathédrale Saint-Pierre and the Reformation Wall. Narrow stone streets, historic buildings, small cafés. The most touristic part of Geneva, but genuinely beautiful in the quiet hours — early morning or late afternoon. The hill is tiring but the views are worth it.

items.name: Carouge
items.description: Technically a separate municipality attached to Geneva. 15 minutes by tram. Italian courtyard architecture, a weekend market, local restaurants. Completely different from the rest of the city's cool and orderly atmosphere. Go to Carouge for dinner; stay there.

items.name: Plainpalais / Jonction
items.description: Student and artist neighbourhood around the University of Geneva. The Plainpalais square turns into the city's best second-hand market on Wednesdays and Saturdays. Jonction is where the Rhône and the Arve meet — where locals swim in summer. The furthest from any tourist atmosphere.

stay.title: Where to Stay

best_time.intro: Geneva lives each season differently. In summer it's the lake; in winter it's the Alps and the silence.

items.label: Spring
items.name: The most balanced time
items.description: From late April to June, Geneva's most balanced period. The lake is still cold but the shore is beautiful. The Jardin Anglais and Parc La Grange are in bloom. Crowds haven't built up yet, flights are cheaper than summer peak. Bike season opens. May is when the city is at its best: not too cold, not too crowded.

callout.label: Parc La Grange — rose garden and lake views
callout.text: On the left bank in Eaux-Vives. Geneva's largest rose garden, in full bloom from late May to early June. Ancient villa, picnic areas, lake views. Free, always open. Overlooked by most tourist maps.

items.subtitle: Spring · Before the crowds, as the city opens up

items.label: Summer
items.name: Lake season
items.description: July and August are the busiest months but the city never feels overwhelming. The lake is ready for swimming. The Geneva Festival in early August — a large fireworks display. Fresh Léman perch instead of fondue; the right choice in summer.

callout.label: Swimming in the river at Jonction
callout.text: Where the Rhône and the Arve meet at Jonction, locals swim in the river in summer. The current is strong; there are safe areas. Entry is free. Local crowd, sun — not a tourist activity, a city summer ritual.

items.subtitle: Summer · Lake, river, open air

items.label: Autumn
items.name: The most underrated season
items.description: September and October: the crowds have gone, the weather is still mild, the lake is calm and blue. Fondue season opens. By late October, Favarger's annual chocolate pots are appearing in confectioners' windows — the first sign of L'Escalade.

callout.label: An autumn evening in Carouge
callout.text: In September and October, Carouge's pavement cafés and restaurants are still outside; the summer crowds have gone. The Wednesday and Saturday market has autumn produce: mushrooms, squash, local cheeses. Go in the late afternoon, walk through the market remnants, sit somewhere. The most relaxed hours in the city.

items.subtitle: Autumn · Lake calm, fondue is back

items.label: Winter
items.name: Silence and the Alps
items.description: December briefly comes alive with the Christmas market and L'Escalade celebrations. January and February are when the city empties of tourists. The Bise wind — cold and sharp from the north — can blow for days; be ready for it. The Alps are close for skiing: Chamonix is an hour away, Les Gets an hour and a half. Geneva in winter is very quiet — the best time for those who like that.

callout.label: L'Escalade — Geneva's most local December moment
callout.text: Every year in the second week of December, a festival marking the 1602 victory over Savoy. A historical procession in costume through the Vieille Ville. Favarger's chocolate pot — Marmite de l'Escalade — made specially for that year, goes on sale in confectioners from mid-November. Tradition: break the pot and share the sweets inside.

items.subtitle: Winter · The city quietens, the Alps are close

monthly_highlights.text: Fêtes de Genève: one of Europe's biggest fireworks shows over the lake; the shore becomes a week-long fairground.
L'Escalade: the celebration of the 1602 victory — costumed parades, history on horseback, and the ritual smashing of the chocolate marmite.
Lake season: swimming at Bains des Pâquis, picnics on the shore; in summer the city lives with its lake.
Ski escape: Chamonix and Portes du Soleil are an hour away; slopes in the morning, fondue in town at night.

best_time.title: When to Go

eat.intro: A city at the heart of Swiss-French cooking. Cheese, freshwater fish, local sausage — all different when eaten in the right place.

local_word.definition: Fresh lake perch fillets from Lac Léman. Geneva's summer dish. If the menu doesn't say 'du Léman', it may not be fresh — look for that label. Lightly floured and fried in butter, served with lemon and rice. May to September.

items.name: Fondue moitié-moitié
items.description: Geneva's classic fondue: half Gruyère, half Vacherin Fribourgeois. Bread pieces dipped in melted cheese with a long fork. The right season for fondue runs from November to March. Avoid the restaurants around Gare Cornavin — they use cheap cheese blends and the difference is noticeable. Bains des Pâquis or restaurants in Carouge are the reliable addresses.
items.tag: Nov–Mar · Bains des Pâquis or Carouge · reservation required

items.name: Raclette
items.description: A half wheel of cheese heated beside the fire, the melted part scraped directly onto the plate. Served with boiled potatoes, cornichons and onions. The electric tabletop version is a shortcut — the real thing is made with a half wheel of cheese.
items.tag: Winter · must be from a half wheel · tabletop version isn't the real thing

items.name: Longeole
items.description: A local sausage unique to Geneva, with protected geographical indication (PDO). Made with pork, fennel seeds and spices; produced nowhere else. One of the city's official dishes. Served with lentils or dried beans. Found at local restaurants in Carouge and at Halles de Rive.
items.tag: Geneva's own PDO · Carouge and Halles de Rive

items.name: Filets de perches du Léman
items.description: Fresh lake perch fillets from Lac Léman — the main dish at lakeside restaurants in summer. If the menu doesn't say 'du Léman', the fish isn't fresh — look for that label. Lightly floured and fried in butter. May to September.
items.tag: May–Sep · du Léman label essential · lakeside restaurants

items.name: Marmite de l'Escalade
items.description: A chocolate pot produced by Favarger each year from mid-November to mid-December. Commemorates the 1602 victory. Filled with small sweets; the tradition is to break it and share the contents. Geneva's most local chocolate experience — unavailable the rest of the year.
items.tag: Mid-Nov to mid-Dec · Favarger · annual production

items.name: Halles de Rive
items.description: In Rive, right next to the lake. Geneva's best covered food market. Local cheese sellers, butchers, fishmongers and bakeries together. Longeole, Gruyère and fresh perch here. Not a tourist destination; this is where Genevans do their shopping. Open every day, busiest in the mornings.
items.tag: Rive · open every day · best in the morning

callout.label: Avoid the area around Gare Cornavin
callout.text: The stretch of Rue du Mont-Blanc around the station has dozens of places serving fondue and raclette. Cheap cheese, thin watery fondue, frozen fish. Avoid these restaurants. Walk a little further: Carouge, Bains des Pâquis, or Les Armures and Café Papon in the Vieille Ville are all much better options.

eat.title: What to Eat

hidden_gems.intro: Just behind Geneva's diplomatic face, a completely different city is waiting.

items.name: La Pointe de la Jonction
items.description: At the western edge of the city, the Rhône and the Arve meet. One is turquoise-green, the other muddy brown — the two colours flow side by side for a long stretch without mixing. Clearly visible to the eye. In summer you can swim in safe areas. Easily reached on foot or by bike. Free, always open.
items.rarity: Two rivers, two colours — flowing side by side without mixing

items.name: Quartier des Grottes
items.description: A few minutes' walk northwest of Gare Cornavin. In the 1980s, residents of a neighbourhood facing demolition occupied their buildings; architects designed organic, wavy, multicoloured façades. Now known as the 'Smurf buildings'. The complete opposite of Geneva's orderly and sterile character. Art studios and alternative cafés in the courtyards. Free, always open.
items.rarity: Switzerland's strangest buildings — the Smurf neighbourhood

items.name: Promenade de la Treille
items.description: Just above the Vieille Ville, along the edge of Parc des Bastions. The wooden bench here, at 120 metres, is among the longest in the world. Each year, the arrival of spring is officially announced by the first bud on the chestnut tree beside this path. Panoramic views over the city, walking distance to the Reformation Wall.
items.rarity: A 120-metre wooden bench and the official announcement of spring

items.name: CERN
items.description: At the western edge of the city, on the Swiss-French border. The world's largest particle physics laboratory and the birthplace of the World Wide Web. Entry to the Science Gateway, opened in 2023, is free — but registration is required. Online registration can be made up to a month in advance and guarantees entry; on-site registration is also possible but subject to availability. Guided tours are also free but open for on-site booking only, two hours before the tour starts — they fill up very quickly. Around 30 minutes by tram.
items.rarity: Where the World Wide Web was born — and the Large Hadron Collider

items.name: Place des Nations — Broken Chair
items.description: In front of the United Nations building, a giant three-legged wooden chair. The fourth leg is broken — representing landmines and unexploded ordnance. Erected temporarily in 1997 to push for the signing of the Ottawa Treaty banning landmines. Geneva never took it down. A guided tour of the Palais des Nations is ticketed, but entry to the square is free.
items.rarity: A sculpture, a treaty — and Geneva never let it go

items.name: Bains des Pâquis
items.description: A wooden jetty extending into the lake on the Pâquis shore. In summer an open-air pool and hammam: swimming, sunbathing, sauna, light food. Doesn't close in winter — one of the most popular spots for winter fondue. Ticketed but reasonably priced. In winter, reservations for fondue are essential; weekends fill up fast.
items.rarity: Swimming, sauna and fondue by the lake — open all year

callout.label: Plainpalais — the city's best second-hand market
callout.text: Every Wednesday and Saturday morning in Plainpalais square. Books, records, vintage clothing, antiques, electronics. Geneva's most colourful and varied open-air market. Best in the early morning. Free entry.

hidden_gems.title: Hidden Gems

items.label: Get the Geneva Transport Card at check-in
items.sub: If you're staying in a hotel, hostel or campsite, you're entitled to it. All public transport free for your stay. Sometimes not sent automatically — always ask.

items.label: See the Jet d'Eau
items.sub: 140 metres into the air, visible from everywhere on the lake. You can walk right up to it. Free.

items.label: Walk to Jonction
items.sub: Where the Rhône and Arve meet in different colours. 25 minutes on foot or by bike. Free.

items.label: Have dinner in Carouge
items.sub: 15 minutes by tram. A completely different Geneva. Local restaurants, courtyards, market remnants.

items.label: Rent a bike from Geneveroule
items.sub: Opposite Gare Cornavin. ID + 20 CHF deposit. Bike is free. Season May–October.

items.label: Go to Bains des Pâquis
items.sub: Swimming and sunbathing in summer, sauna in winter. On the lake, a local spot. Ticketed but affordable.

items.label: See the Reformation Wall
items.sub: In Parc des Bastions. Giant statues of Calvin and the other reformers. Free.

items.label: Visit Halles de Rive
items.sub: Early morning. Local cheese sellers, fishmongers, bakeries. Geneva's real kitchen.

items.label: Visit CERN
items.sub: Science Gateway entry is free, online registration required. Guided tours: on-site booking only, opens 2 hours before, fills fast. Around 30 min by tram.

items.label: Find the Broken Chair
items.sub: In front of the UN building. Fourth leg broken, representing landmines. Entry to the square is free.

items.label: Take the Mouettes
items.sub: Yellow ferry, on your TPG ticket. Crossing the lake.

items.label: Eat in the right place
items.sub: For fondue: Carouge or Bains des Pâquis. For fresh perch: lakeside restaurants. Avoid the Gare Cornavin area.

checklist.title: Geneva Checklist
checklist.completion_message: You've seen Geneva properly — not just the surface.

traps.title: Skip the Traps
traps.intro: Geneva has few traps — but the prices themselves can be one. Know these four and protect your Swiss budget.

items.name: Taking a taxi from the airport
items.description: Paying 40 francs for a taxi when a 7-minute train exists is the city's classic tourist mistake — and the train ticket is free in the baggage hall.
items.instead: Take the free 80-minute ticket from the machine by the baggage belts; at your hotel, ask for the free Geneva Transport Card.

items.name: A 'Swiss watch' from a souvenir shop
items.description: Some of the cheap 'Swiss made' watches and knives in the Rue du Mont-Blanc windows are imported imitations.
items.instead: For the real thing go to an authorised dealer; for a budget gift, Swiss chocolate is always the right answer.

items.name: Insisting on fondue in summer
items.description: It sits on menus year-round, but fondue is a winter dish; served to tourists in August it loses both its taste and its setting.
items.instead: In summer eat filets de perche from the lake; save fondue for a cold evening and a stone-walled brasserie.

items.name: Turning the lake into a paid package
items.description: Expensive 'city tour' packages sell a route that is already free: the Jet d'Eau view, the lakeside, the Old Town.
items.instead: The yellow 'Mouettes' water taxis cross the lake free with your transport card; your feet handle the rest.

callout.label: The golden rule
callout.text: You're in one of the priciest cities on earth, but its best things are free: the lake, the mountain views, the Old Town, a Bains des Pâquis sunset. Save the money for food and chocolate.

itinerary.title: Ready-Made Routes
itinerary.intro: If you hate planning, follow these flows. The times are flexible; keep the spirit, break the order.

plans.title: If You Have 1 Day
plans.subtitle: The lake, the Old Town and the meeting of two rivers

steps.title: Lakeside + Jet d'Eau
steps.description: From the English Garden past the flower clock to the 140-metre fountain; in morning light the lake is a mirror.

steps.title: Old Town + St-Pierre
steps.description: Cobbled lanes, the lake view from the cathedral tower, and the world's longest wooden bench on the Treille.

steps.title: Lunch at Halles de Rive
steps.description: Cheese, charcuterie and fresh pasta at the covered market's stalls; where locals actually lunch.

steps.title: The streets of Carouge
steps.description: Geneva's Greenwich Village: Sardinian-style courtyards, artisan shops, quiet cafés.

steps.title: Bains des Pâquis
steps.description: Swim from the pier in the middle of the lake, or just sit; sunset here is democratic — the same view for everyone.

steps.title: Pâquis evening
steps.description: World kitchens in the city's most colourful quarter — or, if it's winter, fondue by a stone wall.

plans.title: If You Have 3 Days
plans.subtitle: Live the city as a guest, not a tourist

steps.title: Lake and Old Town
steps.description: The 1-day flow above: the shore, the cathedral, Carouge, Pâquis.

steps.title: Science and diplomacy
steps.description: CERN in the morning (free, with reservation), the Place des Nations and the Broken Chair in the afternoon, the Gaudí-esque houses of Les Grottes on the way back.

steps.title: La Jonction and goodbye
steps.description: Walk to the two-coloured meeting of the Rhône and the Arve, the Plainpalais flea market at noon (Wed/Sat), a last Mouettes crossing at dusk + chocolate shopping.

phrases.title: The 5-Word Survival Kit
phrases.intro: Geneva speaks French, but the Swiss way: calm, polite, and with words of its own.

items.meaning: Hello — the mandatory first word of every exchange
Thank you — you'll hear it constantly in Switzerland
Please — add it to the end of your order
Cheers! — white wine glasses rise to this
The friendly greeting of French-speaking Switzerland — both hello and goodbye
